title: Moving after a trade
objectives: Move your quote after being lifted or hit.

screens.title: Lifted
screens.prose: You quote 9.5 at 11.5 on three dice, fair value 10.5. The interviewer buys 2 at your ask. You are now short 2, so you lose if the dice come up high.
screens.question: What do you do with your next quote?

options.text: Move both prices down, to sell more.
options.why: Selling more makes you shorter. You want to buy back, so make your bid more attractive by moving up.

options.text: Widen both sides and keep the centre.
options.why: Widening just trades less. It does nothing to help you buy back the 2 you owe.

options.text: Keep the same quote: the dice have not changed.
options.why: The dice have not changed, but your position has. Short 2, you now want sellers more than buyers.

hints.text: Short 2, do you now want to buy or to sell?
You want sellers to hit a higher bid.
Move both prices up, so buying back is likely and selling more is not.

feedback.correct: Up: a higher bid attracts sellers, and a higher ask slows buyers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You are short, so you want to buy back.

byKey.down: You moved with the trade. Lower prices invite more buyers and make you shorter still.

explain.text: Short 2, you lose if the total is high. A higher bid invites sellers, so you buy back. A higher ask slows buyers, so you sell less.

screens.title: Quote follows position
screens.prose: A simple rule moves your quote with your position. Slide your position and watch the quote. Negative means short.
screens.question: When you are short 2, how has the quote moved from 9.5 at 11.5?

options.why: Slide the position to −2 and read the caption. Short positions push the quote up.
The width stays 2 at every position. Only the centre moves.
Set the position to −2 and read the caption again.

hints.text: Set the slider to −2 and compare with 9.5 at 11.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to −2 and read the caption.

explain.text: At −2 the quote reads 10 at 12, so both sides rose 0.5. Each unit short lifts the quote 0.25, and each unit long lowers it. The width never changes.

screens.title: Skew
screens.prose: Moving both prices together is a **skew**. Your position is your **inventory** $q$. The rule centres your quote on $m = V - \gamma q$, as in the microstructure course. Here $V = 10.5$, $\gamma = 0.25$ a unit and the half-width is 1.
screens.question: You sold 2, so $q = -2$. Set your new quote.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the centre $m$, then go 1 either side.

byKey.down: You moved down. With $q = -2$, $-\gamma q = +0.5$, so the quote goes up.
byKey.nomove: Your bid has not moved. The skew moves both prices.
byKey.width: Your width is not 2. Keep the half-width at 1 around the new centre.

explain.text: $m = 10.5 - 0.25 \times (-2) = 11.0$. One either side gives 10 at 12. The skew is a step of 0.25 for each unit you hold.

screens.title: Four trades
screens.prose: The interviewer trades four times, each time 1 at your current quote. After each trade, fill in your position and your new bid. Your ask is always the bid plus 2.
screens.question: Fill in the position and the new bid after each trade.

hints.text: Lifted means you sold, so the position falls by 1.
Each unit short lifts the centre 0.25.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Update the position first, then $m = 10.5 - 0.25q$.

explain.text: Each lift takes the position down 1 and the quote up 0.25. The hit at 10 buys one back and the quote falls 0.25. Notice each trade happens at the quote you showed just before it.

screens.title: Hit, hit, lifted
screens.prose: Start flat at 9.5 at 11.5 with the same skew rule. The interviewer sells you 1, sells you 1 again, then buys 1. Each trade is at your skewed quote at the time.
screens.question: What is your P&L at fair after the three trades, in pounds?

hints.text: The second buy at 9.25 earns 1.25; the sale at 11.00 earns 0.50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add what each trade earns against 10.50.

byKey.noskew: You used 9.5 and 11.5 for every trade. The skew moved the later prices.
byKey.last: That is the last trade alone. Add the two purchases.
byKey.sign: Every trade was on the right side of 10.50, so the total is positive.

explain.text: The buys at 9.50 and 9.25 earn £1 and £1.25. The skew lowered the ask to 11.00, so the sale earns £0.50. The skew gave up a little edge to cut the position.

screens.title: Keep selling?
screens.prose: The interviewer has lifted you three times, so you are short 3. A colleague says: "They keep buying, so lower our quote and sell them more." The rule is $m = 10.5 - 0.25q$, half-width 1.
screens.question: Where should your quote go?

options.why: You moved the quote down, with the trades. You are short 3 and want to buy back, so move up.
You left the quote where it was. Short 3, you carry risk the skew should start to shed.
Raising only the ask slows buyers but does not invite sellers. Move the bid up too.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $m$ with $q = -3$.

byKey.down: You followed the flow down. Each sale makes you shorter, and a rising total then costs more.

explain.text: With $q = -3$ the centre is $10.5 + 0.75 = 11.25$, so quote 10.25 at 12.25. Moving down would invite even more buying and grow the short. Skew against your inventory, never with it.

screens.title: Two reasons
screens.prose: Now an unknown number, say the floors in a tower. You think 200 and quote 180 at 220. The interviewer, who may know more, lifts your 220.
screens.question: Select all that apply: why should you raise your quote?

options.text: Their buy suggests the value is above what you thought.
You are now short, and lose if the value is high.
You want to sell them more at a higher price.
options.why: Selling more adds to your short. You raise the quote to buy back, not to sell more.

options.text: The trade shows your quote was too wide.
options.why: A buy at your ask says nothing about being too wide. If anything, it hints the quote was too low.

hints.text: One reason is about what the trade tells you, one about what you now hold.
Information moves your fair value; inventory moves your centre.
Both the information and the inventory point up.

feedback.correct: Information and inventory both point up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the reason about value and the reason about position.

byKey.more: Selling more makes you shorter. The move is to buy back.
byKey.tight: Being lifted is evidence about the value, not about the width.

explain.text: A buyer at 220 may know the count is higher, so your fair value rises: that is information. You are also short, which loses if the count is high: that is inventory. Both move the quote up.

screens.title: A trade with no information
screens.prose: Back to three dice. The interviewer says: "I have not looked at anything. I am buying at random." They lift your 11.5 once. The skew rule is unchanged.
screens.question: What is your new ask?

widget.accept: 11.75: fair stays 10.5 and the centre moves to 10.75.
widget.label: Ask

hints.text: Which reason to move still applies?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep fair at 10.5 and skew for $q = -1$.

byKey.nomove: You did not move. The trade carried no information, but you are still short 1.
byKey.info: You moved fair value up as if the buyer knew something. They told you they do not.
byKey.down: You moved down. Short 1, the skew moves the quote up.

explain.text: No information means the fair value stays 10.5. Inventory still moves the centre to $10.5 + 0.25 = 10.75$. The new quote is 9.75 at 11.75.

screens.title: The skew rule
screens.prose: You moved the centre against your position each time. With fair value $V$, skew $\gamma$ a unit, position $q$ and half-width $h$: $$m = V - \gamma q, \qquad \text{bid} = m - h, \qquad \text{ask} = m + h.$$ News moves $V$; trades move $q$.
screens.question: Three dice, $\gamma = 0.25$, $h = 1$. You are long 4. What is your bid?

byKey.sign: You moved the centre up. Long positions push the quote down.
byKey.centre: That is the centre. The bid sits one below it.

explain.text: $m = 10.5 - 0.25 \times 4 = 9.5$, so the bid is 8.5 and the ask 10.5. Long 4, you now sell at fair value to shed risk. That is the zero-edge trade from the last lesson.

screens.title: The ask as a formula
screens.prose: Keep $V = 10.5$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and $h = 1$. Write your ask for any position $q$.
screens.question: Your ask, in terms of $q$:

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the half-width to $m = 10.5 - 0.25q$.

byKey.sign: You added the skew. A long position should lower the ask, so it is $-0.25q$.
byKey.bid: That is the bid. The ask adds the half-width.

explain.text: The ask is $m + h = 10.5 - 0.25q + 1 = 11.5 - 0.25q$. At $q = -2$ it gives 12, as you set. At $q = 0$ it is the plain 11.5.

screens.title: Skew in code
screens.prose: Put the rule in code, then run a whole sequence of trades. Each trade happens at your quote of the moment, then your position changes.
screens.question: Complete `skewed_quote` and `quote_path`.

widget.starter:
def skewed_quote(fair, half_width, gamma, position):
    """Return (bid, ask) centred on fair - gamma * position."""
    ...


def quote_path(fair, half_width, gamma, trades):
    """trades: +1 when you buy one (hit), -1 when you
    sell one (lifted). Return the opening quote and
    the quote after each trade, as a list."""
    ...
widget.solution:
def skewed_quote(fair, half_width, gamma, position):
    """Return (bid, ask) centred on fair - gamma * position."""
    m = fair - gamma * position
    return (m - half_width, m + half_width)


def quote_path(fair, half_width, gamma, trades):
    """trades: +1 when you buy one (hit), -1 when you
    sell one (lifted). Return the opening quote and
    the quote after each trade, as a list."""
    q = 0
    path = [skewed_quote(fair, half_width, gamma, q)]
    for t in trades:
        q += t
        path.append(skewed_quote(fair, half_width, gamma, q))
    return path
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Quotes compare with `math.isclose`, element by element.

hints.text: Start the list with the flat quote, then append one quote after each trade.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the sign of the skew and that the list starts with the opening quote.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: `skewed_quote` is the rule in one line. `quote_path` reuses it after every change in position, so the four trades from the table give the positions and bids you filled in. With `gamma = 0` the quote never moves.

screens.title: After a fund buys calls
screens.prose: You make markets in a share's calls at £2.40 bid, £2.50 ask. A fund buys 2,000 calls from you in one trade. Your desk skews £0.005 for each 100 calls held.
screens.question: What is your new ask, in pounds?

widget.accept: £2.60: short 20 lots lifts the centre £0.10, to £2.55.
widget.label: Ask in pounds

hints.text: How many lots of 100 are you short?
Short 20 lots: the centre moves up $20 \times 0.005 = 0.10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Short 20 lots moves the centre up £0.10 from £2.45.

byKey.down: You moved the quote down. Short calls lose if the share jumps, so move up.
byKey.nomove: That is your old ask. Short 2,000 calls, the skew must move it.

explain.text: Short 2,000 calls is $q = -20$ lots, so the centre rises £0.10 to £2.55. The new quote, £2.50 at £2.60, invites sellers and slows buyers. It is the dice rule with a real position.

ideas: After a trade, move both prices: up after being lifted, down after being hit.
Two reasons to move: the trade is information about value, and your inventory is risk.
Centre on $m = V - \gamma q$: short 2 with $\gamma = 0.25$ moves the centre from 10.5 to 11.

formula.name: Skewed quote
formula.tex: m = V - \gamma q, \qquad \text{bid} = m - h, \quad \text{ask} = m + h
formula.note: $q$ is your position: positive long, negative short.

summary.trap: Lowering your quote after being lifted: you are short and want to buy back, so move up.

quiz.prose: Three dice, fair 10.5, half-width 1, skew 0.25 a unit. The interviewer sells you 1 three times.
quiz.question: What is your new ask?

byKey.sign: You moved up. You are long, so move down.
byKey.nomove: That is the flat ask. You are long 3 now.

explain.text: Long 3 gives $m = 10.5 - 0.75 = 9.75$, so the ask is 10.75. Your ask now sits just above fair value. You are keen to sell.

quiz.prose: On a contract with fair value 50 you quote 49 at 51. You are now long 5.
quiz.question: Which new quote fits a skew for your position?

options.why: You moved up. Long 5, you want to sell, so move down.
You widened instead of moving. The centre should fall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Long means move down.

explain.text: Long 5, you lose if the value falls. Moving both prices down invites buyers and slows sellers. The width stays 2.

quiz.prose: Three dice, fair 10.5. You sold 2 at 12, then bought 1 at 10.
quiz.question: What is your P&L at fair, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark each trade at 10.5.

byKey.one: You counted the sale as 1 unit. You sold 2, each earning 1.5.
byKey.cash: That is your cash, 24 − 10. You still owe 1 unit worth 10.5, so take it off.

explain.text: The sale earns $2 \times 1.5 = 3$ and the purchase at 10 earns 0.5. The total is £3.50, and you are short 1. Say both aloud.

quiz.prose: The interviewer says they trade at random and know nothing. They lift your ask.
quiz.question: Which reason to move your quote still applies?

options.why: They told you they know nothing, so the trade carries no information.
Without information, only the position has changed.

options.text: Neither: random trades need no move.
options.why: The trade was random, but your short position is real.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changed: your view of the value, or your position.

explain.text: A random buyer tells you nothing about value, so fair value stays put. Your position did change, so the skew still applies. Move up by one step.
